question.stem: Inspect the slide query `db.students.find({ age: { $gt: 16, $lt: 10 } })`; why does this range filter evaluate to an empty result set across all numeric `age` values?

options.A: Because chaining `$gt` and `$lt` inside the same field object applies an implicit logical AND, and no number can be simultaneously greater than `16` and less than `10`
options.B: Because MongoDB forbids placing more than one comparison operator inside a single field filter
options.C: Because `$gt` and `$lt` only operate on string fields rather than numeric fields
options.D: Because `find()` requires an explicit `$or` wrapper whenever two comparison operators are used

answer.explanation: Multiple operator conditions inside the same field object (`{ $gt: 16, $lt: 10 }`) are evaluated as a conjunction (logical AND). Since no scalar number is strictly greater than 16 and strictly less than 10 at the same time, the predicate is unsatisfiable (`{ $gt: 10, $lt: 16 }` or `{ $gt: 16, $lt: 20 }` is needed for a valid range). (Key Takeaway: Multiple comparison operators on one field form an implicit AND range condition.)

question.stem: A database administrator needs to empty 10 million records from `students` while preserving custom JSON schema validators and secondary B-tree indexes; which command is architecturally sound?

options.A: `db.dropDatabase()` followed by `use schoolDB`
options.B: `db.students.drop()`
options.C: `db.students.deleteMany({})`
options.D: `db.students.deleteOne({})`

answer.explanation: `db.students.deleteMany({})` deletes every document in the collection while retaining the collection container, validation rules, and secondary indexes. In contrast, `db.students.drop()` destroys the collection along with all its indexes and validation metadata. (Key Takeaway: Use `deleteMany({})` to purge documents when collection metadata and indexes must persist.)

question.stem: Which query pipeline correctly implements deterministic Page 3 retrieval (`5` records per page, ordered from highest to lowest `grade`, returning only `name` and `grade` without `_id`)?

options.A: `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 }).sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`
options.B: `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1 }).sort({ grade: 1 }).skip(15).limit(5)`
options.C: `db.students.findOne({}, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 }).sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(10).limit(5)`
options.D: `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 }).sort({ grade: -1 }).skip(5).limit(10)`

answer.explanation: For Page 3 at 5 records per page, the first 2 pages (`2 * 5 = 10` records) must be skipped via `.skip(10)` and capped at `.limit(5)`. Ordering highest to lowest requires `.sort({ grade: -1 })`, and returning only `name` and `grade` requires `{ name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 }`. (Key Takeaway: Page $k$ of size $N$ uses `skip((k-1)*N).limit(N)` chained on a sorted `find()` cursor.)

mindmap.node_name: Standard Pagination Idiom (Chaining sort().skip(offset).limit(pageSize) for robust page traversal)

question.stem: When evaluating `db.students.find({ $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] })`, which student record will be excluded from the returned cursor?

options.A: `{ name: "Rahul", age: 16 }`
options.B: `{ name: "Meera", age: 18 }`
options.C: `{ name: "Aditi", age: 19 }`
options.D: `{ name: "Kabir", age: 21 }`

answer.explanation: The `$or` operator evaluates to true if at least one sub-condition in its array matches (`age >= 19` OR `name == "Rahul"`). `{ name: "Meera", age: 18 }` fails both conditions (`18 < 19` and `"Meera" != "Rahul"`), so it is excluded. (Key Takeaway: Logical `$or` excludes a document only when every sub-condition in its array evaluates to false.)

mindmap.node_name: Logical Disjunction ($or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] evaluates to true if either sub-clause matches)

question.stem: What architectural risk arises if an engineer runs `db.dropDatabase()` immediately after connecting to a MongoDB deployment without verifying the active session context?

options.A: `db.dropDatabase()` executes strictly against whichever database is currently selected in the session and permanently deletes it without undo capability
options.B: `db.dropDatabase()` automatically drops every user database across the entire server cluster at once
options.C: `db.dropDatabase()` only deletes empty databases and leaves populated collections untouched
options.D: `db.dropDatabase()` moves collections to the `local` recycle partition for 30 days

answer.explanation: `db.dropDatabase()` takes no database-name parameter; it operates strictly against the currently selected database context and permanently purges all of its collections and documents with no undo mechanism. (Key Takeaway: Always verify the active `use <databaseName>` context before invoking irreversible `db.dropDatabase()`.)

mindmap.node_name: Irreversible Deletion Invariant (Deletion cannot be rolled back or undone once confirmed by storage engine)

question.stem: Suppose an application inserts `{ name: "Aditi", grade: 8 }` via `db.students.insertOne()` without supplying an `_id` field; how does MongoDB guarantee document identity?

options.A: MongoDB rejects the insert until an explicit integer primary key is provided
options.B: MongoDB uses the `name` field as the immutable primary key by default
options.C: MongoDB automatically generates and assigns a unique 12-byte `ObjectId` to the `_id` field
options.D: MongoDB stores the document without any `_id` field until `updateOne()` is called

answer.explanation: Every MongoDB document requires a unique `_id` primary key; when omitted during `insertOne()` or `insertMany()`, MongoDB automatically allocates a unique 12-byte `ObjectId` for `_id`. (Key Takeaway: Omitted `_id` fields are automatically populated with a unique 12-byte `ObjectId` on insert.)

question.stem: Why does `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1 })` still return three fields (`_id`, `name`, and `grade`) per document instead of only two?

options.A: Because MongoDB always includes the `_id` primary key field in projections by default unless `{ _id: 0 }` is explicitly specified
options.B: Because `grade: 1` automatically pulls in all numeric metadata fields
options.C: Because an empty query filter `{}` overrides the second projection argument
options.D: Because `find()` requires at least three fields in every returned cursor batch

answer.explanation: In MongoDB projections, the `_id` field is included by default (`_id: 1`) even when an inclusion whitelist like `{ name: 1, grade: 1 }` is specified; suppressing it requires explicitly adding `_id: 0`. (Key Takeaway: The `_id` field is projected by default unless explicitly excluded with `_id: 0`.)

question.stem: An ingestion microservice needs to persist 500 heterogeneous student profiles (`{ name: "Meera", grade: 7 }`, `{ name: "Rahul", grade: 9, subjects: ["Math"] }`) with minimal network roundtrips; which design is optimal?

options.A: Execute 500 sequential `db.students.insertOne()` calls inside a client loop
options.B: Pass all 500 documents as a single array into `db.students.insertMany([...])`, leveraging polymorphic BSON schema support in one batch call
options.C: Run `db.createCollection()` 500 times before inserting each document
options.D: Use `db.students.updateMany({}, { $push: ... })` on an empty collection

answer.explanation: `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` transmits an array of documents in a single batch call and natively supports heterogeneous document structures within the same collection without pre-declaring columns. (Key Takeaway: `insertMany()` minimizes network roundtrips while supporting polymorphic document schemas.)

question.stem: Which compound query expression selects students whose `grade` is neither `7` nor `8` AND whose `age` is strictly less than `19`?

options.A: `db.students.find({ $or: [{ grade: { $in: [7, 8] } }, { age: { $lte: 19 } }] })`
options.B: `db.students.find({ grade: { $ne: [7, 8] }, age: { $gt: 19 } })`
options.C: `db.students.find({ $and: [{ grade: { $nin: [7, 8] } }, { age: { $lt: 19 } }] })`
options.D: `db.students.find({ grade: { $nin: [7, 8] }, age: { $lte: 19 } })`

answer.explanation: `$nin: [7, 8]` matches documents whose `grade` is not in `[7, 8]`, `$lt: 19` enforces strictly less than `19` (unlike `$lte: 19`), and wrapping both inside `$and: [...]` enforces logical conjunction. (Key Takeaway: Combine `$nin` for array exclusion and `$lt` for strict upper bounds inside `$and`.)

question.stem: If a developer mistakenly runs `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { age: 20 })` in modern MongoDB instead of wrapping `{ age: 20 }` inside `{ $set: { age: 20 } }`, why is the `$set` operator critical?

options.A: Because `updateOne()` requires atomic update operators such as `$set` to modify target fields in place without overwriting the entire document
options.B: Because `$set` is the only operator capable of filtering by `{ name: "Rahul" }`
options.C: Because omitting `$set` automatically drops the `students` collection
options.D: Because `$set` converts `updateOne()` into a multi-document `updateMany()` operation

answer.explanation: `updateOne(filter, update)` requires update operators like `$set`, `$inc`, `$push`, or `$pull` in its second argument so that specific fields are modified in place without replacing unreferenced fields of the document. (Key Takeaway: `updateOne()` relies on update operators like `$set` for targeted in-place field mutation.)
